messages.subject: [statnet_help] goodness-of-fit confusion
messages.body_plain:
greetings,

i am very confused about an issue i am encountering with statnet's "gof" 
function, and i am hoping someone can help. thus far, my knowledge about 
statnet is based entirely on reference guides (as well as the help of a 
few experts who have been very generous with their time). the references 
i have been using regarding gof are:

1) statnet's internal help function (help(gof))

2) the online user's guide on the statnet website 
(http://csde.washington.edu/statnet/tutorial.shtml)

3) the "statnet tutorial" from sunbelt XXVI (goodreau, handcock, hunter, 
butts), also downloaded from the statnet website.

i am using R version 2.5.1 on windows vista, with an updated version of 
statnet. the network i am attempting to model contains 1640 nodes, and 
is undirected. per steven goodreau's advice, i always use 
proposaltype="TNT" for both the "ergm" function and the "gof" function 
due to the large size of my network.

my confusion arises from the following: let's assume my model is called 
"model", and i want my gof object to be called "fit". statnet's 
help(gof) function indicates that my gof command should look like this: 
*fit <- gof(model)*. (more specifically, i have been using 
*fit=gof(model,nsim=10,proposaltype="TNT"*.) i then enter 
*par(mfrow=c(1,3))* followed by *par(oma=c(0.5,2,1,0.5))* followed by 
*plot(fit)* to see all three plots at the same time. so far, this has 
been producing three plots with pretty horrible fit.

in contrast, both the online user's guide and the sunbelt tutorial 
indicate that my gof command should look like this: *fit <- 
gof(model~degree)*. (more specifically, i have been using 
*fit=gof(model~degree,nsim=10,proposaltype="TNT"*.) i then enter 
*plot(fit)* to see the degree distribution plot, and i can repeat this 
using "dist" or "espartners" for the others. using this method, i get 
plots with MUCH better fit.

which is the proper method to use? the first produces results that seem 
almost too bad to be true, and the second produces results that seem 
almost too good to be true.

thanks in advance,

kevin lewis
kmlewis@fas.harvard.edu

would be helpful to see.

thanks greatly!

-kevin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] addendum
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

Thanks for your emails.  You've identified a situation where we haven't 
kept our help files up to date with changes in statnet.

The way to generate a gof object in the latest versions of statnet is 
using the formula notation, e.g. gof(model~degree).  We hadn't changed it 
in the documentation, but I will add that to our list of things to do with 
high prioirity.  I just explored the function that is called when one uses 
a separate GOF argument (gof.ergm) and found a bug created by a change in 
code elsewhere. I will be sure to have that method removed (since the 
functionality is really redundant between the two), unless users have a 
strong preference for keeping it in as well. Users?

On to the issue of why your runs seem almost too good to be true when 
using the correct syntax. I suspect that if you increase the interval 
argument for the gof (i.e. the number of steps between successive 
samples), then you will find the fit decline dramatically.  The default 
value for interval is good for small networks, but needs to be increased 
for large networks.  Probably there just insn't enough time for the chain 
to wander too far away from the observed network given your size.  From 
the runs you sent, it seems clear to me that your model is not fitting 
well, so I do think the gof results you're getting *are* too good to 
actually be true.

Let us know if this doesn't resolve your questions.

Cheers,
Steve
